records.name: Aspazija
records.facts_used: The catalogue connects Aspazija with Greek aspasios, explained as “longed for, pleasant, beloved”. In Latvian cultural history it is also a literary pseudonym. A writer’s pseudonym and the later use of the same spelling as a given name are distinct kinds of evidence. The Latvian National Library records Aspazija as the author of the 1904 edition of Zeltīte, a drama in two acts published by Gulbis in St Petersburg. That bibliographic record already predates the catalogue’s 1925 personal-name example; the latter cannot be treated as the first occurrence of the literary name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: The established 1904 bibliographic claim is reused from round21, not fetched/researched again. The catalogue’s 1925 record is not claimed as earliest use: it postdates the literary pseudonym. The unsupported wife-of-Pericles wording is omitted. Checked location: Catalogue p. 72 for aspasios; previously reviewed round21 LNB object60960 bibliography (1904 edition of Zeltīte). Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Paulius
records.facts_used: Salys explains Paulius as a Lithuanian form connected directly with Latin Paulus, alongside the older Povilas tradition transmitted through Slavic forms. He explicitly rejects treating Paulius as a modern purist invention: it already occurs in early Lithuanian records. He quotes the exact first name Paulius in the 1570 Babtai inventory, in the record Paulius Rimuidowicz. He also cites Klein’s 1653 grammar. These are dated records reported by a later linguistic study, rather than a first birth registration or newly inspected archival originals.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: 1570 is an inventory record quoted by Salys, not independently inspected archive or first birth; surname not modernized in quotation. Checked location: PDF 144 / printed 129: Latin-form versus Povilas discussion, 1653 grammar and 1570 Babtai inventory Paulius Rimuidowicz. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Skirgaila
records.facts_used: Skirgaila is an older Lithuanian personal name. Maciejauskienė places it among Lithuanian-origin names with a second component gail- and discusses Gailas as a conversational short form. This records the name’s structure without imposing a single literal translation on the whole compound. Salys discusses the medieval prince Skirgaila acquiring the Christian name Ivan, keeping the two names in their historical context. His calendar for 1964 separately prints Skirgaila (Skiras) on 15 January. The modern calendar entry does not date the beginning of the older personal name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Accepted text is an attested historical personal-name and renaming account, not a new lexical compound derivation; no forced strong/pity or battle translation. Salys’s baptism chronology remains attributed/qualified. Checked location: Salys PDF 48 / printed 33: older personal name and Christian name Ivan before 1384 (qualified); dictionary PDF 266 / printed 251; Maciejauskienė PDF 7 / printed 90. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Snieguolė
records.facts_used: Snieguolė is formed from Lithuanian sniegas, “snow”, with a diminutive suffix. The word also has a flower-name use, and Snieguolė is the Lithuanian name for Snow White. These associations do not identify which one motivated every individual family’s choice. The dictionary explicitly gives Sniega as a short form of Snieguolė; the historical calendar for 1964 prints Snieguolė (Sniega) on 15 January. Together they document the exact long and short names, without claiming that the name was invented in 1964.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Word, flower and Snow White contexts do not establish every family’s naming motive; no date of invention asserted.
